extracted.intended_audience: fantasy and science fiction writers (novelists), especially those working with multiple POV characters
extracted.subtask_description: A practical guide for SFF writers on using third-person point of view effectively: choosing the right 3rd-person variant, avoiding craft pitfalls (like head-hopping), maintaining distinct POV voices, and organizing multi-POV plots and worldbuilding so continuity holds across a sprawling novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third person POV definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Third person POV is a narrative perspective in which the story is told by an external narrator using 'he,' 'she,' or 'they' pronouns, as opposed to first person ('I') or second person ('you').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quick-answer framing: third person places the narrator outside characters' direct speech; it's the dominant perspective in epic fantasy and space opera. Use this definition as the baseline when deciding narrative framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose the correct 3rd-person variant (limited / omniscient / objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three main variants: third person limited (follows one character closely at a time), third person omniscient (narrator knows everything), and third person objective (reports only observable actions and dialogue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use third person limited for contemporary epic fantasy (balances intimacy and scope). Third person omniscient can convey world history and multiple inner lives but risks feeling distant or 'telling.' Third person objective is rare but powerful for unreliable or mysterious POV characters. Consider your story's needs (scale, intimacy, reliability) when selecting a variant; examples given include Tolkien (frequent omniscient dips) and modern limited-use examples like Joe Abercrombie.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use third person when you need worldbuilding breadth, multiple storylines, scale, or villain/antagonist chapters
rubrics_metrics.description: Third person allows the narrator to convey world details a character might take for granted, move between characters chapter-by-chapter, and portray large-scale, world-altering events; it also makes antagonist/ villain chapters more manageable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your story requires conveying background, multiple simultaneous locations, or large-scale events (or if you want to enter morally complex villain minds while keeping narrative distance), third person is the practical choice. Treat these reasons as selection criteria when choosing POV for SFF subgenres like epic fantasy and space opera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor each scene to a single POV character; avoid head-hopping
rubrics_metrics.description: Head-hopping occurs when viewpoint shifts within a scene or chapter without a clear break, jumping between characters' inner experiences and breaking immersion. Rule of thumb: in third person limited, each scene should be anchored to a single POV character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: narrating a secondary character's thoughts in the middle of a protagonist's chapter. Fixes: don't delete the information—have the anchored POV character infer or observe it instead, or move the material to the other character's chapter or a scene break. Use this as a hard craft constraint for limited POV sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor each chapter immediately to the POV
rubrics_metrics.description: The first paragraph (ideally the first line) of any third-person limited chapter should establish whose perspective we're in as quickly and clearly as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is especially important in multi-POV novels to prevent reader confusion. Anti-pattern: making readers wait half a page before they can work out whose perspective they're following. Use a clear, immediate anchor (name, distinct sensory detail, or voice cue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage multiple POV arcs with strong organization and timeline control
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple POV characters in different locations or times create continuity risks: characters may learn things at different times, timelines can be non-linear, and intersecting arcs can require precise sequencing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat multi-POV as an organizational problem as well as a craft one. Use purpose-built worldbuilding tools (example: World Anvil's Timelines feature) to track when events happen relative to each other, and to prevent plot-continuity disasters (e.g., accidental reveals, duplicated or contradictory events). Pay special attention to non-linear timelines, flashbacks, and parallel timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain distinct voices across POV characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Each POV character should shape not only what the narration describes but its tone, vocabulary, and focus—so that different characters read differently from one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the 'same narrator, different names' problem. Make a gruff soldier's narration blunt and physical; make an aristocratic mage's narration more analytical and historically aware. Exercise: take a paragraph and ask 'Would my protagonist notice or describe this this way?'; if yes, voices may be too similar. Use diction, sensory focus, and internal priorities to differentiate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use psychic distance deliberately
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychic distance is how close the narrative voice is to the character's inner experience, ranging from detached/omniscient to deep interiority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use closer psychic distance for emotionally intense moments (deep interior thoughts, immediate sensations) and more distant narration when you need to convey plot information or shift tone. Third person limited allows you to vary distance within a single POV; be intentional about where you place the camera for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filter worldbuilding through character perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: World details should be presented as the POV character would notice them, not as a textbook delivered by the narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: treating worldbuilding as exposition the narrator dumps. Instead, have the POV character react to or selectively notice aspects of the world according to their background, interests, and experience (a local might not remark on the floating towers; a newcomer would). This both reveals character and avoids info-dumping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let information gaps create tension
rubrics_metrics.description: In third person limited, the POV character can only know what they've witnessed, been told, or can reasonably infer; these gaps are a source of dramatic tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist letting the POV character have implausible knowledge that removes stakes. Use constraints on knowledge to generate vulnerability and suspense. Where readers know more from other POVs, manage how and when that information is revealed to avoid undermining character decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be intentional with free indirect discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Free indirect discourse blends narrator voice and character thought without tags (e.g., 'The plan was doomed; anyone could see that'), and is a powerful tool in third person limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use free indirect discourse to get intimacy without first-person narration, but be careful: it can slide into ambiguous attribution and accidental head-hopping if the boundary between narrator opinion and character thought isn't clear. Always decide whether a line is the narrator's assessment or the character's private thought and signal it through tone, lexical choice, or scene anchoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe subgenre-specific POV conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Different SFF subgenres have conventions around POV: epic fantasy and space opera usually favor third person (often multiple POVs); urban fantasy often prefers first person; grimdark favors close third person aligned with morally compromised perspectives; LitRPG trends toward first person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use subgenre expectations as a guide, not a rule. If you write against convention (e.g., LitRPG in third person), be aware readers' expectations and the tonal effects. Study exemplar works (cited authors: Tolkien, Joe Abercrombie, Patrick Rothfuss, Ann Leckie) to see how POV conventions are used successfully in each subgenre.
